## Who he is

Roger Federer (born 8 August 1981 in Basel, Switzerland) turned professional in
1998 and retired from competitive tennis in September 2022 at the Laver Cup in
London. Over a 24-year career he won 20 major singles titles, spent a record 237
consecutive weeks ranked World No. 1, and became the first man to win 100 or more
tour-level singles titles in the Open Era after Jimmy Connors.

Beyond the trophies, Federer is remembered for a one-handed backhand, an
efficient all-court game, and a demeanour that made him a global ambassador for
the sport. His rivalries with Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic defined men's
tennis for nearly two decades.

> "I fear no one, but I respect everyone." — Roger Federer

# Career

From a junior Wimbledon champion in 1998 to a farewell at the 2022 Laver Cup.

## Timeline

| Year | Milestone |
|------|-----------|
| 1998 | Wins the Wimbledon boys' singles title; turns professional. |
| 2001 | Ends Pete Sampras's 31-match Wimbledon win streak in the fourth round. |
| 2003 | Wins his first Grand Slam title at Wimbledon. |
| 2004 | Wins three majors in a season and reaches No. 1 for the first time (2 February 2004). |
| 2006 | Goes 92–5 on the season, reaching all four major finals. |
| 2009 | Completes the Career Grand Slam by winning the French Open; breaks Sampras's record of 14 majors at Wimbledon. |
| 2012 | Wins a seventh Wimbledon title and returns to No. 1, extending his record for weeks at the top. |
| 2017 | Wins the Australian Open and Wimbledon at age 35 after a six-month injury layoff. |
| 2018 | Defends the Australian Open for a 20th and final major title; briefly returns to No. 1 at age 36, the oldest man to hold the ranking. |
| 2019 | Loses a five-set Wimbledon final to Novak Djokovic after holding two championship points. |
| 2021 | Plays his final competitive singles matches at Wimbledon. |
| 2022 | Retires at the Laver Cup in London, playing a farewell doubles match alongside Rafael Nadal. |

## Weeks at World No. 1

Federer first reached No. 1 on 2 February 2004 and held the position for 237
consecutive weeks through 17 August 2008 — a record that still stands. He
reclaimed the top ranking several times, most improbably in 2018 at age 36. His
total of 310 weeks at No. 1 was a record until surpassed by Novak Djokovic.

| Ranking record | Detail |
|----------------|--------|
| Total weeks at No. 1 | 310 |
| Consecutive weeks at No. 1 | 237 (record) |
| Year-end No. 1 finishes | 5 (2004–2007, 2009) |
| Years in the top 10 | 14 consecutive (2002–2016), then 2017–2020 |

## ATP titles since 2018

Federer's last eight tour-level titles all came in 2018 and 2019, including his
100th career title in Dubai. He reached finals afterward but did not win another
title before retiring; 2020, 2021, and 2022 produced none.

## Surface strengths

Federer won titles on every surface but built his legend on fast courts. He was
especially dominant on grass, where he won 8 Wimbledon titles and 10 Halle
titles, and on indoor hard courts, where he won his home event in Basel 10 times.
His lone French Open title in 2009 completed the Career Grand Slam and came the
year Rafael Nadal was upset before the final.

## Playing style

- **One-handed backhand** — a signature shot, refined late in his career into an
  aggressive weapon after coaching work with Ivan Ljubičić.
- **Serve** — not the fastest on tour, but among the most accurate and
  disguised, letting him hold serve cheaply for two decades.
- **Movement** — widely praised footwork that kept points short and reduced wear
  on his body, contributing to his longevity.
- **SABR** — the "Sneak Attack By Roger," a chip-charge return off second serves
  he introduced in 2015.

## Signature matches

**2008 Wimbledon final (lost).** Often called the greatest match ever played,
Federer lost 6–4, 6–4, 6–7, 6–7, 9–7 to Rafael Nadal in near-darkness, ending his
five-year reign at the All England Club.

**2009 Wimbledon final (won).** A 16–14 fifth set against Andy Roddick delivered
Federer's 15th major, moving him past Pete Sampras for the all-time men's record
at the time.

**2017 Australian Open final (won).** Returning from a knee injury and unseeded
in the draw's expectations, the 35-year-old beat Nadal in five sets for a first
major in nearly five years.

**2019 Wimbledon final (lost).** Federer held two championship points on serve at
8–7 in the fifth before losing 13–12 (7–3) in the first Wimbledon final decided
by a final-set tie-break.

## Olympic and team results

- **2008 Beijing** — Olympic gold in doubles with Stan Wawrinka.
- **2012 London** — Olympic silver in singles, losing the final to Andy Murray.
- **2014** — Led Switzerland to its first Davis Cup title.
- **2001, 2018** — Won the Hopman Cup for Switzerland.

# Rivalries

The "Big Three" and the matches that shaped an era. For most of Federer's prime,
men's tennis was defined by three players — Federer, Rafael Nadal, and Novak
Djokovic — who between them won the overwhelming majority of majors from 2005
onward. Federer was the elder of the group, and his head-to-head records against
the other two tightened as the younger men matured.

## Federer vs. Nadal

:::

Nadal led the overall rivalry 24–16, an edge built largely on clay, where he beat
Federer 14–2. On grass and hard courts the two were far closer. Their nine
Grand Slam finals include the 2008 Wimbledon final — widely regarded as the
greatest match ever — and the 2017 Australian Open final, which Federer won in
five sets during his late-career resurgence. They closed the rivalry as friends,
partnering in doubles at the 2017 Laver Cup and again at Federer's farewell in
2022.

## Federer vs. Djokovic

The most-played rivalry of the Open Era at 50 matches, with Djokovic leading
27–23. Djokovic repeatedly ended Federer's runs at the majors, including the
2010 and 2011 US Open semi-finals — the latter after Federer held two match
points — and the 2014 and 2019 Wimbledon finals. Federer had his best success
indoors and at the year-end championships.

Federer beat Andy Murray in all three of their Grand Slam finals (2008 US Open,
2010 Australian Open, 2012 Wimbledon), but Murray took the biggest prize between
them by winning the 2012 Olympic singles gold on Centre Court just weeks after
losing the Wimbledon final there.

## Earlier-era rivals

- **Andy Roddick** — Federer led 21–3 and beat Roddick in four major finals, all
  at Wimbledon or the US Open.
- **Lleyton Hewitt** — after an early even split, Federer won 18 straight to
  finish 18–9.
- **Pete Sampras** — met once, in the 2001 Wimbledon fourth round, which the
  19-year-old Federer won in five sets to end Sampras's title defence.

# Legacy

Influence on and off the court.

## On the court

Federer's career reset expectations for how long a tennis player could stay at
the top. He won majors 15 years apart (2003 and 2018), reached World No. 1 at age
36, and played Grand Slam quarter-finals into his 40th year. His 237 consecutive
weeks at No. 1 and his run of 10 straight Grand Slam finals (2005–2007) remain
records.

Stylistically, he is credited with reviving belief in the one-handed backhand and
in aggressive, forward-moving all-court tennis at a time when the sport was
trending toward baseline attrition. A generation of players — Grigor Dimitrov,
Stefanos Tsitsipas, and others — modeled their games on his.

## Sportsmanship and popularity

Federer won the ATP's Stefan Edberg Sportsmanship Award, voted by players, a
record number of times, and the Laureus World Sportsman of the Year award five
times. He also won the ATP Fans' Favourite award every year from 2003 through
2022 — an unbroken 19-year run — reflecting a level of cross-border popularity
rare in an individual sport.

## Philanthropy

The **Roger Federer Foundation**, established in 2003, focuses on early childhood
education in southern Africa and in Switzerland. By his retirement the foundation
reported reaching well over one million children through education programs,
funded in part by exhibition matches such as the "Match for Africa" series, which
featured opponents including Rafael Nadal and Bill Gates.

## Business

- **On** — Federer took an equity stake in the Swiss running-shoe company in
  2019, helped design its "The Roger" lifestyle line, and became a public face of
  the brand as it grew into a multibillion-dollar business.
- **Laver Cup** — Federer's management company, Team8, co-founded the Laver Cup
  in 2017, a Ryder Cup–style Europe vs. World team event now sanctioned by the
  ATP. He chose it as the setting for his retirement.
- **Endorsements** — long-term partnerships with Rolex, Mercedes-Benz, Lindt,
  Credit Suisse, Wilson, and Uniqlo, the last on a reported 10-year deal signed
  in 2018.

## Retirement

Federer announced his retirement on 15 September 2022 and played his final match
six days later at the Laver Cup in London — a doubles rubber partnered with
Rafael Nadal against Frances Tiafoe and Jack Sock. The team lost, but the image
of Federer and Nadal in tears holding hands afterward became one of the defining
photographs of modern sport.

> "Tennis has treated me more generously than I ever would have dreamt, and now I
> must recognize when it is time to end my competitive career." — Roger Federer,
> retirement letter, 2022
